task.goal: Invent a small traveling exhibit that invites children and adults to compare how everyday objects are repaired across generations.
hard_constraints: One curator has six weeks, three display cases and existing donated objects with uneven documentation.
No fabricated provenance, live tools, electrical power or mandatory phone interaction.
Objects must stay protected; every interaction needs a seated and low-reading alternative; test against ordinary labels.
task.available_resources: Object photos, repair notes where documented, printable cards.
task.expected_result: A feasible exhibit concept and critique plan.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Repair Detectives: Compare the Evidence
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Three cases organize donated objects around visible repair features: joining, replacing and reinforcing. Include only categories supported by the actual collection; a case may instead show two contrasting repairs of the same kind. Visitors compare protected objects with enlarged photographs and select a printable card showing the feature they noticed. Turning the card reveals a documented explanation, or explicitly says that the repair method, date or repairer is unknown.

The mechanism is close observation followed by evidence checking. Children and adults can contribute equally before discussing whether they recognize similar repairs from their own lives. A short invitation asks, “Who has seen something repaired this way?” Generational comparisons emerge from visitors’ accounts; the exhibit never assigns an undocumented object to a particular generation. Accounts remain personal recollections, separate from collection evidence.

One curator can spend the first week auditing notes and photographs, two weeks choosing comparisons and writing evidence statements, one week making paper prototypes, and two weeks testing and preparing the traveling set. Requirements are the three cases, existing objects, photographs and printed cards. No objects leave their cases during interaction.

Every activity has a duplicate card set readable from a seated position, with large photographs, simple symbols and an optional pointing response. Position cases for seated viewing where possible; photographs provide equivalent inspection when object details are difficult to see. The main uncertainty is whether photographs reveal enough to support meaningful comparison. If they do not, reduce the number of comparisons rather than invent explanations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype one comparison with six mixed-age pairs. Alternate whether pairs first see ordinary factual labels or the detective cards, using matched objects and equal time. Ask each pair to identify one visible difference, distinguish a known fact from an unknown, and share a generational comparison if they have one. Check the seated, pointing-only version too. Revise or abandon the mechanism if cards produce more guessing or false certainty without improving observation or exchange over labels.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Two Memories, One Object
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Each case becomes a conversation prompt about an everyday repair experience represented by the donated objects. Possible themes include learning a repair, deciding whether something is worth repairing, and living with a visible patch. Choose themes after reviewing the collection. Each object receives a brief ordinary label containing only supported facts, with uncertainty stated plainly.

The primary mechanism is reciprocal storytelling: two visitors answer the same prompt, then identify one similarity and one difference. Printable turn cards prevent an adult’s account from automatically becoming the authoritative answer. Prompts might ask, “Who helped you when something broke?” or “Show which mattered most: time, money, appearance or keeping a memory.” A visitor without a repair memory can describe a present preference; no one must pretend to represent an entire generation. Solo visitors can compare two occasions in their own life.

Cards use large pictures, a short phrase and a pointing option. All prompts and object photographs are available at seated height outside the cases. Visitors can silently select and compare picture cards instead of reading aloud or telling a story. Objects remain protected throughout, and visitor accounts are neither collected nor converted into provenance.

Implementation needs only an evidence audit, three compact prompt sets, printed photographs and a labeled traveling packet. Within six weeks, the curator can develop and test one case before reproducing the format across all three. The approach assumes visitors are willing to exchange personal experiences. It may reveal differences within generations more strongly than differences between them; that is a legitimate finding rather than a failure to enforce a historical narrative.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Try one case with six mixed-age pairs, alternating ordinary labels alone and labels plus conversation cards across comparable objects. Observe whether both people contribute and whether they articulate a specific similarity or difference. Offer a silent, seated pointing version and check whether it supports the same comparison. Ask whether either participant felt pushed to speak for their age group. Simplify or reject the cards if labels produce equally balanced, specific exchanges or the prompts repeatedly create discomfort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The Repair Choice Table
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Three cases anchor three paper decision activities: “What matters?”, “What could change your choice?” and “What happened here?” Each uses protected donated objects and their photographs. Visitors place or point to printed priority cards—such as time, cost, appearance, continued use and sentimental value—beside a photograph, then choose among clearly labeled hypothetical responses: repair, seek help, keep without using, replace or remain undecided. No technical procedure or tool use is offered.

The mechanism is making tradeoffs visible. Visitors first choose independently, then compare priorities with someone of another generation when available. A second card changes one explicitly hypothetical condition, such as access to a skilled helper or needing the object tomorrow. Visitors can revise their choices and discuss whether differences reflect age, experience or circumstances. Finally, a reveal card presents whatever is actually documented about the object’s repair; it does not claim to explain the original owner’s motives unless the notes support that claim.

The curator needs enough collection evidence to anchor at least a few examples, but historical prices, dates and repairer biographies are unnecessary. Printed priorities, scenario cards, photographs and short evidence labels fit into a small traveling packet alongside the three cases. Audit and selection take one week, drafting and paper prototyping two, with the remaining three for visitor checks, revision and packing instructions.

Each interaction is duplicated for seated use and supports pointing to large pictures rather than reading or handling cards. Objects stay enclosed. The limitation is that hypothetical choices reveal visitors’ reasoning, not actual historical repair behavior; the exhibit must keep that distinction explicit.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Test a single scenario with six mixed-age pairs against an ordinary-label version using a comparable object. Ask visitors to explain one choice and one difference between their priorities. Then ask which statements describe documented history and which are hypothetical. Include seated, low-reading trials. The mechanism fails if visitors confuse scenarios with provenance, if priorities do not generate specific comparisons, or if ordinary labels support equally useful discussion with less effort.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Pass the Repair: A Paper Teaching Relay
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Visitors become repair teachers using printed models beside three protected cases. Each case connects an everyday donated object to a simplified paper representation of a repair, selected only after auditing the objects and notes. For example, where the collection supports it, visitors can arrange printed patch shapes over a pictured tear. Loose cards represent parts; there are no tools, adhesives, powered elements or handling of collection objects.

The mechanism is skill transmission through demonstration and imitation. One visitor privately chooses an arrangement, demonstrates it without speaking, and invites a partner to recreate it with a duplicate card set. They then swap teaching roles. Comparing the two demonstrations makes different habits visible: where someone starts, what they emphasize and how they communicate. An optional final prompt asks whether either approach resembles something learned from an older or younger person. Visitors need not claim repair expertise or represent their generation. Solo visitors can reproduce a printed example, then demonstrate a different arrangement to a companion later.

Each case clearly separates documented object evidence from the paper exercise. The exercise models placement and communication, not repair strength, safety or an undocumented historical procedure. Without sufficient documentation, it must not present a sequence as the way the displayed object was repaired.

All activities work seated, use large pictures and support silent pointing instead of moving cards. Duplicate object photographs provide seated inspection. The curator needs printable model sets, evidence labels and packing instructions. Allow one week for the audit, two for one prototype and selection, one for visitor checks, and two for revision and production across three cases.

The main prerequisites are visibly understandable repair examples and visitors willing to demonstrate. The limitation is substantial: this reveals how repair knowledge can pass between people, while historical differences require documented evidence or explicitly personal recollection.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Prototype one case with six mixed-age pairs. Give half ordinary factual labels and half the same labels plus the relay, with equal visiting time. Check whether both participants contribute and can identify a specific difference in how they demonstrated or understood the repair. Ask what the exercise establishes about the historical object; treating a paper arrangement as historical fact counts against the design. Include seated, silent, pointing-only participation. Reject or simplify the relay if it mainly tests memory or dexterity, generates unsupported historical claims, or produces no richer cross-generation comparison than ordinary labels.

DIRECT_FULL.title: How Many Lifetimes in One Repair?
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The exhibit uses time alignment to make repair across generations visible. Beside three protected cases, printed timelines place documented repair events against familiar spans: a school year, ten years and a human lifetime. A repair that seems recent to an adult may predate a child’s birth. Visitors compare when repairs happened, whether an object was repaired repeatedly, and which generations could have encountered it before or after a repair.

The cases address three questions: “When was it repaired?”, “Was it repaired again?” and “What can’t we date?” Assign objects only where their documentation supports the question. A clearly visible present-day endpoint prevents an old repair date from implying continuous use. Undated repairs appear in a separate photograph panel, never at guessed positions on the timeline. Object age, repair date and documented use receive distinct symbols.

Visitors point to broad, optional birth-period bands on a duplicate tabletop timeline, then locate the same repair relative to each person’s lifetime. Neither exact ages nor personal stories are required. Large photographs, picture-based time spans and a short worked example provide a seated, low-reading route through every comparison. All collection objects remain enclosed; interaction uses only printed material.

The necessary assumption is that the donation records contain at least two reasonably dated repair events or repair intervals. The first-week audit is a feasibility gate: without those anchors, this concept should be rejected. One curator can spend weeks two and three preparing timelines and checking every date against its source, week four prototyping, and weeks five and six revising and packing the three-case exhibit. Requirements are existing cases, objects, photographs, notes and printed sheets. Chronology can reveal overlap and succession; it cannot establish that an entire generation preferred a particular repair method.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Test one timeline with six child–adult pairs, dividing pairs between the timeline and ordinary labels containing the same facts. Ask each pair to locate a repair relative to both lifetimes and identify one supported comparison. Check whether visitors mistakenly infer continuous use or assign undated repairs to an era. Include seated, pointing-only trials. Reject or simplify the timeline if it causes those errors, requires repeated explanation, or adds no clearer comparison than ordinary labels. This small check identifies design failures; it cannot establish broad effectiveness.

EXPAND.title: Pass the Repair On
EXPAND.proposal:
The exhibit turns repair knowledge into a short communication relay. At each of three cases, one visitor studies a photograph and a documented repair description, then explains it to a partner using words, gestures or picture cards. The partner arranges printed pictures to represent the explanation. Both then uncover the source card and see what survived the handover. Partners exchange roles at the next case.

The mechanism is teaching followed by reconstruction: visitors experience how explanations preserve or lose practical knowledge. Across generations, the comparison concerns how each person explains and understands the same repair, without assuming older visitors possess greater expertise. A closing prompt asks which picture, word or gesture made the explanation clearer. The activity concerns understanding repairs, not performing them.

This requires at least one donated object with a sufficiently documented repair method. Three objects are preferable, but the other cases can show related objects whose missing documentation is explicitly acknowledged. Do not invent missing steps or use a successful reconstruction as evidence that a procedure is technically sound. If no repair method is documented, this concept is unsuitable.

One curator can audit the evidence in week one, select and simplify descriptions in weeks two and three, prototype in week four, and test and pack in weeks five and six. Materials are existing objects, enlarged photographs, source cards and loose picture cards. Objects remain enclosed. Each relay has a seated version using duplicate photographs and large pictures; pointing can replace speaking, reading or arranging. The host must provide seats. The main uncertainty is whether the documentation supports explanations simple enough for children without becoming misleading.
EXPAND.experiment: Prototype one relay with four mixed-age pairs. Compare it with ordinary labels for a second, comparably documented repair, reversing the order for half the pairs. Ask both partners to describe how the repair holds or replaces something, and identify what remains unknown. Include a seated, pointing-only round. Reject the relay if it introduces unsupported steps, repeatedly gives one partner control, or produces poorer understanding than labels. Inspect whether both generations actually contribute to the explanation.

EXPAND.title: Design a Paper Repair Signature
EXPAND.proposal:
Each case pairs a protected repaired object with an enlarged photograph and a paper design surface. Visitors create a proposed visible repair for a pictured break using printable patch, seam, binding or replacement-piece shapes. They then place their design beside a partner’s and beside the object photograph. Every visitor design is prominently marked “imagined,” while labels identify only what is known about the real repair.

The mechanism is expressive making: externalizing a repair idea gives people something concrete to compare before discussing it. A child and adult might both bridge a break but differ in whether they emphasize symmetry, decoration or concealment. The prompt is “Show how you would make this repair look,” rather than a technical challenge. Visitors compare the visible treatment of damage across their own designs and the collection; no design is presented as safe, functional or historically typical.

The approach needs photographs with clearly visible repair features and enough space on a printed sheet for two compositions. It does not require repair dates or repairer biographies. Its limit is equally clear: the results reveal present aesthetic approaches across participating generations, not historical changes in repair practice. Ordinary evidence labels must retain that distinction.

The curator can spend one week selecting objects, two creating reusable paper shapes and short labels, one prototyping, and two checking access and preparing the traveling packet. All pieces are printable; there are no adhesives, cutting activities or tools for visitors. Objects stay inside the three cases. Duplicate photographs and large shapes support seated use. Visitors can point while a companion positions pieces, or simply choose between pictured compositions. The host supplies seating. Designs need not be collected or displayed beyond the visit.
EXPAND.experiment: Give four mixed-age pairs one paper design activity and one comparable object with ordinary labels, alternating order. Ask each pair to identify a specific similarity and difference in how repairs are made visible. Check whether they can distinguish their imagined design from the donated object’s documented repair. Try the seated, pointing version. Drop the activity if conversation remains about decoration without connecting to repairs, if visitors infer false historical claims, or if labels produce equally specific comparisons with less effort.

EXPAND.title: A Repair in Your Words
EXPAND.proposal:
The three cases become a small translation workshop about repair language. Beside each protected object, visitors find an enlarged repair photograph and an invitation to name or describe what they see. A child and adult each offer a word, phrase, gesture or selected picture. They then match their expressions to the same visible feature and compare them with a short, evidence-based museum description.

The mechanism is translation between vocabularies. Different words can conceal shared knowledge, while the same word can refer to different actions. Asking visitors to establish what each expression means makes those differences inspectable. Someone might describe a repair as “sewn,” “patched,” or “held together”; the photograph anchors discussion of whether those descriptions concern the same feature. The museum description supplies clarity without grading family language as inferior.

No expression is attributed to an age group unless supported by evidence. Participants speak for themselves, and the exhibit makes no claim that a word originated in their generation. If the repair method is undocumented, the museum card describes visible features and states that the method is unknown. This makes the concept viable with uneven documentation, although photographs must reveal enough detail to discuss.

Within six weeks, one curator can audit the objects, choose three clear examples, prepare picture and phrase cards, test one case, then reproduce and pack the format. Requirements are photographs, printed cards and the existing cases. Each activity has duplicate materials usable while seated, with large images and pointing or gesture alternatives to reading and speech. The host supplies seating. Participation requires no writing or retained visitor contributions. A limitation is that differences may reflect language, household or experience more than generation; that possibility should remain visible.
EXPAND.experiment: Try the workshop with four mixed-age pairs, comparing one case with an ordinary-label case and reversing the order between pairs. Ask whether each person can explain their partner’s description and locate the feature it names. Check whether any participant feels corrected or stereotyped. Include seated, picture-only participation. Reject the mechanism if it mainly tests vocabulary, leaves visitors unable to explain the repair, or adds no useful exchange beyond ordinary labels.

EXPAND.title: The People Behind a Repair
EXPAND.proposal:
Each case anchors a paper map of how repair knowledge and help travel between people. Visitors place or point to picture cards around an object photograph: myself, household member, friend, neighbor, repair business, community group, or unknown. Using an everyday object they have actually encountered, each participant traces who noticed the problem, who knew what to do, and who carried out the repair. A partner from another generation builds a second map, and they compare the routes.

The mechanism is relationship mapping. Making the chain visible can reveal that apparently individual repairs depend on someone who recognizes a fault, teaches a technique, supplies a part or performs the work. The comparison concerns how repair gets accomplished across participants’ generations, rather than which repair they would choose. A visitor without a repair experience can inspect a companion’s map and identify an unanswered question; they need not invent a memory.

Maps are explicitly personal accounts, separate from collection evidence. Each object label identifies any documented repairer or helper and otherwise says “We do not know who helped repair this.” The exhibit never transfers a visitor’s network onto a donated object. This approach assumes enough visitors have repair experiences to map; it may expose household differences more strongly than generational ones.

One curator can audit and select objects in week one, develop one picture-based map format in weeks two and three, prototype in week four, then test and prepare all three cases in the remaining weeks. Materials are printed photographs, role cards and map sheets. Objects remain protected. Large role pictures support seated, low-reading participation through pointing, with no requirement to write, speak publicly or disclose names. Duplicate sets work on visitors’ laps; the host supplies seats. No accounts need to be collected.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare the map activity with ordinary labels using four mixed-age pairs and comparable objects, alternating order. Look for a concrete comparison about who enabled a repair and how knowledge reached the repairer. Check that visitors distinguish their account from the object’s history. Test a seated, pointing-only version. Reject or simplify the maps if people cannot recall relevant examples, the roles exclude common experiences, or ordinary labels elicit equally specific comparisons with less explanation.

EXPAND.title: Guess the Repair’s Age
EXPAND.proposal:
Visitors encounter the three cases as a dating puzzle: does a repair’s appearance reliably tell us when it was made? Each protected object has an enlarged photograph and a short factual label, with the repair date initially available on a separate reveal card. Visitors point to a broad period on a printed timeline, or choose “cannot tell,” before checking the documented answer. Object manufacture dates and repair dates are explicitly distinguished.

The primary mechanism is prediction followed by chronological correction. A visibly rough repair might look old to one visitor and recent to another; placing the documented repair on the timeline makes those expectations discussable. Children and adults predict independently, then compare which clues influenced them. Neither participant represents an entire generation. A closing prompt asks whether they recognize the technique from their own lifetimes, keeping personal recollection separate from collection evidence.

This concept requires an initial evidence gate: at least three repairs with defensible dates or bounded date ranges, spanning at least two periods relevant to generational comparison. Donation dates alone do not qualify. Undated objects can appear as explicitly unresolved examples, but cannot supply the chronological reveal. If the audit finds insufficient evidence, this alternative is unsuitable; visual appearance must never substitute for provenance.

One curator can audit documentation in week one, select examples and define honest date ranges in week two, prepare photographs, timelines and reveal cards in weeks three and four, and test, revise and pack in weeks five and six. Each case needs only existing objects and printable materials. Duplicate large photographs, pictorial period markers and pointing responses provide seated, low-reading participation; the traveling instructions require host seating. Objects remain enclosed throughout. The principal uncertainty is whether the collection contains enough dated repairs—and whether their dates challenge expectations enough to sustain discussion.
EXPAND.experiment: Prototype one comparison using qualifying objects. Alternate the puzzle and ordinary labels containing the same facts across eight child–adult pairs, four per format. Afterward, ask each pair to point out one repair comparison and distinguish what is documented from what they guessed. Observe whether both participants contribute. Revise or reject the puzzle if it produces no clearer comparison than ordinary labels, excludes the younger participant, or leaves visitors treating appearance as proof of age. This is a small usability critique, not evidence of a general audience effect.

The main prerequisites are visibly understandable repair examples and visitors willing to demonstrate. The limitation is substantial: this reveals how repair knowledge can pass between people, while historical differences require documented evidence or explicitly personal recollection.
REFINE.experiment: Prototype one case with six mixed-age pairs. Give half ordinary factual labels and half the same labels plus the relay, with equal visiting time. Check whether both participants contribute and can identify a specific difference in how they demonstrated or understood the repair. Ask what the exercise establishes about the historical object; treating a paper arrangement as historical fact counts against the design. Include seated, silent, pointing-only participation. Reject or simplify the relay if it mainly tests memory or dexterity, generates unsupported historical claims, or produces no richer cross-generation comparison than ordinary labels.

REFINE.title: Repair Detectives: Compare One Repair Across Two Lives
REFINE.proposal:
Original candidate 0 is the strongest fit: protected objects, visible evidence and printable cards make its observation-and-checking mechanism feasible for one curator in six weeks. Its consequential weakness is that “Who has seen something repaired this way?” can produce isolated anecdotes without any comparison across generations.

Replace that invitation with one reciprocal comparison card per case. After inspecting and checking a visible repair feature, each visitor indicates whether they have encountered a similar repair: yes, different or unfamiliar. Visitors with an example briefly describe how the object was repaired and who did it; partners then identify one similarity or difference between their examples. If only one has an example, compare that recollection with the displayed repair, using only what is visible or documented. Mark the two sources explicitly: “Object evidence” and “Personal memory.” This makes generational exchange a concrete action while preserving close observation followed by evidence checking.

Use the same short prompt and large photographic choices at all three cases. Provide duplicate photographs and cards for seated use, with pointing sufficient to compare visible features; speaking and card handling remain optional. Objects stay enclosed. No tools, power or phones are needed. Substitute this card during the existing drafting and prototype weeks rather than adding another activity.

Prerequisites are at least one clearly photographed repair feature and mixed-generation visitors for a cross-generation exchange. Remaining limit: recollections reveal individual experiences, not representative historical trends; visitors without relevant memories can still compare evidence but cannot supply a lived comparison.
REFINE.experiment: Prototype one case with six mixed-generation pairs: two see ordinary factual labels, two the original detective invitation, and two the revised comparison card, with equal time and the same object. Include seated, pointing-only participation. Record whether both visitors contribute, whether they identify a specific repair similarity or difference, and whether they distinguish memory from object evidence. The repair fails its initial check if the revised card produces only recognition or unsupported historical claims, or if its picture choices cannot support a specific comparison without spoken explanation. Use this small trial to revise the card, not to claim a proven audience effect.

SAVE.title: Repair Detectives: Compare the Evidence
SAVE.proposal:
Three cases organize donated objects around visible repair features: joining, replacing and reinforcing. Include only categories supported by the actual collection; a case may instead show two contrasting repairs of the same kind. Visitors compare protected objects with enlarged photographs and select a printable card showing the feature they noticed. Turning the card reveals a documented explanation, or explicitly says that the repair method, date or repairer is unknown.

The mechanism is close observation followed by evidence checking. Children and adults can contribute equally before discussing whether they recognize similar repairs from their own lives. A short invitation asks, “Who has seen something repaired this way?” Generational comparisons emerge from visitors’ accounts; the exhibit never assigns an undocumented object to a particular generation. Accounts remain personal recollections, separate from collection evidence.

One curator can spend the first week auditing notes and photographs, two weeks choosing comparisons and writing evidence statements, one week making paper prototypes, and two weeks testing and preparing the traveling set. Requirements are the three cases, existing objects, photographs and printed cards. No objects leave their cases during interaction.

Every activity has a duplicate card set readable from a seated position, with large photographs, simple symbols and an optional pointing response. Position cases for seated viewing where possible; photographs provide equivalent inspection when object details are difficult to see. The main uncertainty is whether photographs reveal enough to support meaningful comparison. If they do not, reduce the number of comparisons rather than invent explanations.
SAVE.experiment: Prototype one comparison with six mixed-age pairs. Alternate whether pairs first see ordinary factual labels or the detective cards, using matched objects and equal time. Ask each pair to identify one visible difference, distinguish a known fact from an unknown, and share a generational comparison if they have one. Check the seated, pointing-only version too. Revise or abandon the mechanism if cards produce more guessing or false certainty without improving observation or exchange over labels.

SAVE.title: Two Memories, One Object
SAVE.proposal:
Each case becomes a conversation prompt about an everyday repair experience represented by the donated objects. Possible themes include learning a repair, deciding whether something is worth repairing, and living with a visible patch. Choose themes after reviewing the collection. Each object receives a brief ordinary label containing only supported facts, with uncertainty stated plainly.

The primary mechanism is reciprocal storytelling: two visitors answer the same prompt, then identify one similarity and one difference. Printable turn cards prevent an adult’s account from automatically becoming the authoritative answer. Prompts might ask, “Who helped you when something broke?” or “Show which mattered most: time, money, appearance or keeping a memory.” A visitor without a repair memory can describe a present preference; no one must pretend to represent an entire generation. Solo visitors can compare two occasions in their own life.

Cards use large pictures, a short phrase and a pointing option. All prompts and object photographs are available at seated height outside the cases. Visitors can silently select and compare picture cards instead of reading aloud or telling a story. Objects remain protected throughout, and visitor accounts are neither collected nor converted into provenance.

Implementation needs only an evidence audit, three compact prompt sets, printed photographs and a labeled traveling packet. Within six weeks, the curator can develop and test one case before reproducing the format across all three. The approach assumes visitors are willing to exchange personal experiences. It may reveal differences within generations more strongly than differences between them; that is a legitimate finding rather than a failure to enforce a historical narrative.
SAVE.experiment: Try one case with six mixed-age pairs, alternating ordinary labels alone and labels plus conversation cards across comparable objects. Observe whether both people contribute and whether they articulate a specific similarity or difference. Offer a silent, seated pointing version and check whether it supports the same comparison. Ask whether either participant felt pushed to speak for their age group. Simplify or reject the cards if labels produce equally balanced, specific exchanges or the prompts repeatedly create discomfort.

SAVE.title: The Repair Choice Table
SAVE.proposal:
Three cases anchor three paper decision activities: “What matters?”, “What could change your choice?” and “What happened here?” Each uses protected donated objects and their photographs. Visitors place or point to printed priority cards—such as time, cost, appearance, continued use and sentimental value—beside a photograph, then choose among clearly labeled hypothetical responses: repair, seek help, keep without using, replace or remain undecided. No technical procedure or tool use is offered.

The mechanism is making tradeoffs visible. Visitors first choose independently, then compare priorities with someone of another generation when available. A second card changes one explicitly hypothetical condition, such as access to a skilled helper or needing the object tomorrow. Visitors can revise their choices and discuss whether differences reflect age, experience or circumstances. Finally, a reveal card presents whatever is actually documented about the object’s repair; it does not claim to explain the original owner’s motives unless the notes support that claim.

The curator needs enough collection evidence to anchor at least a few examples, but historical prices, dates and repairer biographies are unnecessary. Printed priorities, scenario cards, photographs and short evidence labels fit into a small traveling packet alongside the three cases. Audit and selection take one week, drafting and paper prototyping two, with the remaining three for visitor checks, revision and packing instructions.

Each interaction is duplicated for seated use and supports pointing to large pictures rather than reading or handling cards. Objects stay enclosed. The limitation is that hypothetical choices reveal visitors’ reasoning, not actual historical repair behavior; the exhibit must keep that distinction explicit.
SAVE.experiment: Test a single scenario with six mixed-age pairs against an ordinary-label version using a comparable object. Ask visitors to explain one choice and one difference between their priorities. Then ask which statements describe documented history and which are hypothetical. Include seated, low-reading trials. The mechanism fails if visitors confuse scenarios with provenance, if priorities do not generate specific comparisons, or if ordinary labels support equally useful discussion with less effort.

SAVE.title: Pass the Repair On
SAVE.proposal:
The exhibit turns repair knowledge into a short communication relay. At each of three cases, one visitor studies a photograph and a documented repair description, then explains it to a partner using words, gestures or picture cards. The partner arranges printed pictures to represent the explanation. Both then uncover the source card and see what survived the handover. Partners exchange roles at the next case.

The mechanism is teaching followed by reconstruction: visitors experience how explanations preserve or lose practical knowledge. Across generations, the comparison concerns how each person explains and understands the same repair, without assuming older visitors possess greater expertise. A closing prompt asks which picture, word or gesture made the explanation clearer. The activity concerns understanding repairs, not performing them.

This requires at least one donated object with a sufficiently documented repair method. Three objects are preferable, but the other cases can show related objects whose missing documentation is explicitly acknowledged. Do not invent missing steps or use a successful reconstruction as evidence that a procedure is technically sound. If no repair method is documented, this concept is unsuitable.

One curator can audit the evidence in week one, select and simplify descriptions in weeks two and three, prototype in week four, and test and pack in weeks five and six. Materials are existing objects, enlarged photographs, source cards and loose picture cards. Objects remain enclosed. Each relay has a seated version using duplicate photographs and large pictures; pointing can replace speaking, reading or arranging. The host must provide seats. The main uncertainty is whether the documentation supports explanations simple enough for children without becoming misleading.
SAVE.experiment: Prototype one relay with four mixed-age pairs. Compare it with ordinary labels for a second, comparably documented repair, reversing the order for half the pairs. Ask both partners to describe how the repair holds or replaces something, and identify what remains unknown. Include a seated, pointing-only round. Reject the relay if it introduces unsupported steps, repeatedly gives one partner control, or produces poorer understanding than labels. Inspect whether both generations actually contribute to the explanation.

SAVE.title: Design a Paper Repair Signature
SAVE.proposal:
Each case pairs a protected repaired object with an enlarged photograph and a paper design surface. Visitors create a proposed visible repair for a pictured break using printable patch, seam, binding or replacement-piece shapes. They then place their design beside a partner’s and beside the object photograph. Every visitor design is prominently marked “imagined,” while labels identify only what is known about the real repair.

The mechanism is expressive making: externalizing a repair idea gives people something concrete to compare before discussing it. A child and adult might both bridge a break but differ in whether they emphasize symmetry, decoration or concealment. The prompt is “Show how you would make this repair look,” rather than a technical challenge. Visitors compare the visible treatment of damage across their own designs and the collection; no design is presented as safe, functional or historically typical.

The approach needs photographs with clearly visible repair features and enough space on a printed sheet for two compositions. It does not require repair dates or repairer biographies. Its limit is equally clear: the results reveal present aesthetic approaches across participating generations, not historical changes in repair practice. Ordinary evidence labels must retain that distinction.

The curator can spend one week selecting objects, two creating reusable paper shapes and short labels, one prototyping, and two checking access and preparing the traveling packet. All pieces are printable; there are no adhesives, cutting activities or tools for visitors. Objects stay inside the three cases. Duplicate photographs and large shapes support seated use. Visitors can point while a companion positions pieces, or simply choose between pictured compositions. The host supplies seating. Designs need not be collected or displayed beyond the visit.
SAVE.experiment: Give four mixed-age pairs one paper design activity and one comparable object with ordinary labels, alternating order. Ask each pair to identify a specific similarity and difference in how repairs are made visible. Check whether they can distinguish their imagined design from the donated object’s documented repair. Try the seated, pointing version. Drop the activity if conversation remains about decoration without connecting to repairs, if visitors infer false historical claims, or if labels produce equally specific comparisons with less effort.

SAVE.title: A Repair in Your Words
SAVE.proposal:
The three cases become a small translation workshop about repair language. Beside each protected object, visitors find an enlarged repair photograph and an invitation to name or describe what they see. A child and adult each offer a word, phrase, gesture or selected picture. They then match their expressions to the same visible feature and compare them with a short, evidence-based museum description.

The mechanism is translation between vocabularies. Different words can conceal shared knowledge, while the same word can refer to different actions. Asking visitors to establish what each expression means makes those differences inspectable. Someone might describe a repair as “sewn,” “patched,” or “held together”; the photograph anchors discussion of whether those descriptions concern the same feature. The museum description supplies clarity without grading family language as inferior.

No expression is attributed to an age group unless supported by evidence. Participants speak for themselves, and the exhibit makes no claim that a word originated in their generation. If the repair method is undocumented, the museum card describes visible features and states that the method is unknown. This makes the concept viable with uneven documentation, although photographs must reveal enough detail to discuss.

Within six weeks, one curator can audit the objects, choose three clear examples, prepare picture and phrase cards, test one case, then reproduce and pack the format. Requirements are photographs, printed cards and the existing cases. Each activity has duplicate materials usable while seated, with large images and pointing or gesture alternatives to reading and speech. The host supplies seating. Participation requires no writing or retained visitor contributions. A limitation is that differences may reflect language, household or experience more than generation; that possibility should remain visible.
SAVE.experiment: Try the workshop with four mixed-age pairs, comparing one case with an ordinary-label case and reversing the order between pairs. Ask whether each person can explain their partner’s description and locate the feature it names. Check whether any participant feels corrected or stereotyped. Include seated, picture-only participation. Reject the mechanism if it mainly tests vocabulary, leaves visitors unable to explain the repair, or adds no useful exchange beyond ordinary labels.

SAVE.title: The People Behind a Repair
SAVE.proposal:
Each case anchors a paper map of how repair knowledge and help travel between people. Visitors place or point to picture cards around an object photograph: myself, household member, friend, neighbor, repair business, community group, or unknown. Using an everyday object they have actually encountered, each participant traces who noticed the problem, who knew what to do, and who carried out the repair. A partner from another generation builds a second map, and they compare the routes.

The mechanism is relationship mapping. Making the chain visible can reveal that apparently individual repairs depend on someone who recognizes a fault, teaches a technique, supplies a part or performs the work. The comparison concerns how repair gets accomplished across participants’ generations, rather than which repair they would choose. A visitor without a repair experience can inspect a companion’s map and identify an unanswered question; they need not invent a memory.

Maps are explicitly personal accounts, separate from collection evidence. Each object label identifies any documented repairer or helper and otherwise says “We do not know who helped repair this.” The exhibit never transfers a visitor’s network onto a donated object. This approach assumes enough visitors have repair experiences to map; it may expose household differences more strongly than generational ones.

One curator can audit and select objects in week one, develop one picture-based map format in weeks two and three, prototype in week four, then test and prepare all three cases in the remaining weeks. Materials are printed photographs, role cards and map sheets. Objects remain protected. Large role pictures support seated, low-reading participation through pointing, with no requirement to write, speak publicly or disclose names. Duplicate sets work on visitors’ laps; the host supplies seats. No accounts need to be collected.
SAVE.experiment: Compare the map activity with ordinary labels using four mixed-age pairs and comparable objects, alternating order. Look for a concrete comparison about who enabled a repair and how knowledge reached the repairer. Check that visitors distinguish their account from the object’s history. Test a seated, pointing-only version. Reject or simplify the maps if people cannot recall relevant examples, the roles exclude common experiences, or ordinary labels elicit equally specific comparisons with less explanation.
